extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York; citizens and voters considering the proposed Constitution (general educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria for constituting a federal judiciary: how judges should be appointed, their tenure and support, the judiciary's relation to other branches, and the interpretive rules that preserve constitutional supremacy and individual rights. Focused on institutional design to secure independent, competent courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of appointing judges
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner of constituting [the judiciary] embraces the mode of appointing the judges — 'the same with that of appointing the officers of the Union in general.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointment method should follow the general mode used for Union officers; see related discussion in prior papers. The essay treats appointment as one of three core structural questions (mode of appointment; tenure; partition of authority). No single appointment scheme is endorsed here beyond being consistent with the Union's general practice, but later passages warn about particular dangers depending on who appoints (executive, legislature, both, or the people).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure during good behavior (permanency in office)
rubrics_metrics.description: All judges appointed by the United States are to hold their offices 'DURING GOOD BEHAVIOR.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life tenure during good behavior is presented as 'one of the most valuable of the modern improvements' — a barrier to despotism in monarchy and to encroachments by the representative body in a republic. Permanency in office is called 'an indispensable ingredient' and 'in a great measure, the citadel of the public justice and the public security.' The rationale includes promoting steady, upright, and impartial administration of the laws and securing firmness against pressure from the other branches or popular passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisions for judges' support and precautions for responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The tenure question 'chiefly concerns their duration in office; the provisions for their support; the precautions for their responsibility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sufficient financial support and clear measures for responsibility are necessary to prevent dependence on other branches and to secure judicial independence. Support provisions reduce incentives to seek favor from appointing authorities and are part of the structural protections for impartial judging. Specific mechanisms are not enumerated here but are identified as essential alongside tenure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of the judicial power from legislative and executive powers
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is no liberty, if the power of judging be not separated from the legislative and executive powers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A distinct judiciary is required to protect liberty because courts have neither the sword nor the purse. Separation prevents union of judging with either of the other departments, which would enable oppression. The judiciary's proper independence is essential to uphold constitutional limitations and individual rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judiciary as the weakest branch yet requiring protection
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The judiciary is beyond comparison the weakest of the three departments of power' — it has 'neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because courts lack force and will, they are vulnerable to being 'overpowered, awed, or influenced' by the legislature or executive. Institutional protections (tenure, support, separation) are therefore required to enable the judiciary to defend itself and uphold constitutional boundaries despite its comparative weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts' authority to declare legislative acts void (judicial review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts must be able to 'declare all acts contrary to the manifest tenor of the Constitution void.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserving constitutional limitations (e.g., prohibitions on bills of attainder, ex-post-facto laws) depends on courts' power to invalidate contrary statutes. This power rests on the principle that any act of a delegated authority contrary to its commission is void; thus courts should enforce the Constitution as superior law. The essay frames this as necessary, not as implying judicial superiority over the legislature but as fidelity to the people's superior will embodied in the Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges must prefer the Constitution to statutes when they conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The Constitution ought to be preferred to the statute, the intention of the people to the intention of their agents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges, as interpreters, should give effect to the superior obligation of the Constitution over ordinary legislative acts. When an irreconcilable variance exists, the Constitution governs. This is an interpretive duty grounded in the Constitution's status as fundamental law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of construction between conflicting statutes: later statute preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: When two statutes of equal authority conflict, 'the last in order of time shall be preferred to the first.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a conventional rule of statutory construction: among equal authorities, the more recent expression of the authority's will is preferred. Hamilton notes this is a rule adopted by courts as 'consonant to truth and propriety' rather than enacted by positive law, and applies when construing conflicting statutes of the same (equal) source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of construction between superior and subordinate authorities: prior superior act prevails
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In regard to the interfering acts of a superior and subordinate authority... the prior act of a superior ought to be preferred to the subsequent act of an inferior and subordinate authority.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a subordinate statute conflicts with a superior law (e.g., a statute with the Constitution), the superior (prior) law controls and must be adhered to by tribunals. This explains why constitutional provisions take precedence over later legislative enactments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial duty to exercise judgment, not will (avoid substituting pleasure for law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts 'must declare the sense of the law; and if they should be disposed to exercise WILL instead of JUDGMENT... the consequence would... be the substitution of their pleasure to that of the legislative body.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges must follow legal reasoning and established interpretive principles rather than personal preferences. If courts substitute will for judgment, the remedy would be to abolish judges separate from the legislative body — thus impartial legal judgment is a key normative constraint on judicial behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence as safeguard against popular passions and factional impulses
rubrics_metrics.description: Independence of the judges is 'equally requisite to guard the Constitution and the rights of individuals from the effects of those ill humors... which the arts of designing men, or the influence of particular conjunctures, sometimes disseminate among the people themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanent, independent judges act as a check against transient majoritarian impulses and manipulative factions, protecting minority rights and preventing 'dangerous innovations' or 'serious oppressions' enacted in moments of popular excitement. Judges must be insulated from ephemeral public sentiment until the people alter the Constitution by a solemn process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid periodic or temporary judicial appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That inflexible and uniform adherence to the rights of the Constitution... can certainly not be expected from judges who hold their offices by a temporary commission.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodic appointments, however regulated, would undermine independence by creating incentives for complaisance to the appointing branch or to popularity. Temporary tenure would discourage skilled practitioners from accepting the bench and would risk placing justice into less able hands. Therefore, temporary commissions are portrayed as incompatible with dependable constitutional adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications and scarcity of fit characters for the bench (integrity and legal learning)
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be but few men in the society who will have sufficient skill in the laws to qualify them for the stations of judges; even fewer who unite the requisite integrity with the requisite knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of a voluminous code of laws and the need for mastery of precedents, judges require long and laborious study and high integrity. The institutional design (especially tenure) must attract and retain such qualified individuals; without permanency, the government risks less able administrators of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binding role of strict rules and precedents to avoid arbitrary discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: 'To avoid an arbitrary discretion in the courts, it is indispensable that they should be bound down by strict rules and precedents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A large body of precedents helps define judicial duty and restrain arbitrary decisions. Precedent accumulates and demands prolonged study; adherence to established rules channels judicial decision-making and reduces the danger of capricious rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks associated with different appointing authorities (executive, legislature, both, or the people)
rubrics_metrics.description: If appointment power were committed to the Executive or legislature, there would be danger of improper complaisance; if to both, unwillingness to risk displeasure; if to the people, tendency to consult popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different appointing mechanisms create distinct risks to judicial independence: executive or legislative appointers may induce favor; shared appointment may produce undue caution; direct popular appointment may encourage popularity-seeking. The choice of appointing authority therefore must consider and mitigate these tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judiciary's dependence on the executive for enforcement (lack of force)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary 'must ultimately depend upon the aid of the executive arm even for the efficacy of its judgments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because courts lack military or fiscal power, their rulings require executive enforcement. This practical dependence underscores why structural protections (tenure, respect for precedent, constitutional supremacy) are necessary to ensure the judiciary can function effectively despite lacking coercive means.
